common_name: Zuni Crape Myrtle (Compact Lavender-Pink Semi-Dwarf Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Zuni's smaller mature size makes it a good fit for tight residential spaces where larger crape myrtles would eventually crowd the site.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Zuni is one of the smaller National Arboretum hybrid crape myrtles, producing lavender-pink flower clusters from summer into early fall on a compact, semi-dwarf tree well suited to smaller residential landscapes and foundation plantings. Like other National Arboretum hybrids it shows good resistance to powdery mildew, a common disease problem on older Lagerstroemia indica cultivars, and develops attractive exfoliating bark with age. Fall foliage turns shades of orange-red. Remove root suckers as they appear and prune only to remove crossing or dead branches rather than heavily topping the plant.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — National Arboretum Crape Myrtle Program

common_name: Acoma Crape Myrtle (Weeping White Dwarf Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Acoma's gracefully weeping branch habit spreads wider than it grows tall, so allow ample lateral space when siting it.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Acoma is a distinctive weeping, semi-dwarf National Arboretum hybrid crape myrtle with pure white flower clusters produced from summer into fall on gracefully arching branches, a growth habit unusual among crape myrtles that gives it strong specimen and accent value. Like its sibling cultivars it shows good resistance to powdery mildew and develops attractive mottled, exfoliating bark with maturity. Its spreading, weeping form makes it well suited as a small specimen tree, container planting, or bank cover where the arching branches can be shown off. Remove root suckers and prune only lightly to shape rather than heavily topping the plant.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — National Arboretum Crape Myrtle Program

common_name: Biloxi Crape Myrtle (Light Pink Vigorous Gulf Coast Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Biloxi grows quickly into a medium-to-large tree and performs especially well in the humid Gulf Coast climate for which it is named.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Biloxi is a vigorous, medium-to-large National Arboretum hybrid crape myrtle named for the Mississippi Gulf Coast city, producing clear light pink flower clusters over a long summer bloom season on a fast-growing, upright tree. It shows strong resistance to powdery mildew, a common problem for older Lagerstroemia indica cultivars in the humid Gulf South, and develops attractively mottled, exfoliating cinnamon-and-gray bark as it matures. Fall foliage takes on orange to red tones before dropping. Remove root suckers as they appear and prune selectively to remove crossing or dead branches rather than heavily topping the tree, which spoils its natural vase-shaped form.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — National Arboretum Crape Myrtle Program

common_name: Chindo Viburnum (Award-Winning Large Evergreen Screening Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Chindo grows quickly into a dense, large evergreen screen or small tree and is more cold-hardy than the species type, extending its range further north.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Chindo is a selected, more cold-hardy form of sweet viburnum that earned a Gold Medal Award from the Georgia Botanical Garden for its outstanding performance as a large, fast-growing evergreen screen. It has bold, glossy, deep green leaves considerably larger than most viburnums, white spring flower clusters, and showy red fruit that matures to black, all on a dense shrub that quickly reaches privacy-hedge size or can be limbed up into a small multi-trunked tree. It tolerates heat and humidity very well, making it a Gulf South landscape staple for fast screening, and needs only occasional shaping to control size in a smaller garden.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; Gumpo is a very low, spreading Satsuki azalea that blooms later in spring than most azaleas, extending the azalea display into early summer.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun. Gumpo is a classic dwarf Satsuki azalea from Japan, valued for its unusually low, spreading, groundcover-like habit and large flowers relative to its small size, blooming several weeks later in late spring than most other azaleas and extending the azalea season into early summer. Named forms are available in white, pink, and variegated pink-and-white flower colors, all sharing the same compact, mounding growth well suited to low borders, rock gardens, and container culture. Water deeply during dry spells and protect from harsh afternoon sun, which can scorch the foliage; prune lightly right after flowering to shape without removing next year's buds.
